title: Thin air: pressure, blood and VO₂max
goal: Explain why the oxygen pressure of the air falls with altitude, how that lowers SaO₂ and VO₂max, and roughly how much endurance performance you lose per 1,000 m.

steps.title: Thin air, same oxygen share
steps.text:
Climb and [barometric pressure](g:barometric-pressure) falls [[c:alt-pb-falls]]. Air is still 20.9% oxygen at every height ([FiO₂](g:fio2) 0.209), so the [partial pressure](g:partial-pressure) of oxygen falls in proportion [[c:alt-po2-proportional]]. That is [hypobaric hypoxia](g:hypobaric-hypoxia): real altitude. A tent or mask that removes oxygen at normal pressure gives [normobaric hypoxia](g:normobaric-hypoxia) instead.

Inside your airways the air is full of water vapour (47 mmHg), so the oxygen pressure that counts is [PIO₂](g:pio2):

**PIO₂ = FiO₂ × (PB − 47 mmHg)**

| Altitude | PB (mmHg) | PIO₂ (mmHg) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 m | 760 | 150 |
| 2,000 m | 596 | 115 |
| 2,500 m | 560 | 108 |
| 3,000 m | 526 | 101 |
| 4,000 m | 462 | 87 |

Standard-atmosphere values: weather moves them a little. Being [hypoxic](g:hypoxia) at 2,500 m means breathing about 28% less oxygen pressure.

claims.text: Barometric pressure falls as altitude rises.

evidence.quote: With increasing altitude, a progressive reduction in barometric pressure, air temperature and air humidity can be observed

claims.text: The share of oxygen in inspired air stays the same with altitude, so a lower barometric pressure gives a lower oxygen partial pressure.

evidence.quote: In practice, at sea level, O2 constitutes 20.94% of total gas molecules in inspired air, which with a normal rate of alveolar ventilation leads to an alveolar partial O2 pressure of roughly 100 mmHg for a barometric pressure of roughly 760 mmHg.
the same percentage of O2 in the inspired air, combined with a lower barometric pressure and higher rate of ventilation, results in an alveolar partial O2 pressure of roughly 67 mmHg

steps.title: PIO₂ at 2,000 m
steps.problem: At 2,000 m, PB is about 596 mmHg. What is PIO₂, and how far below sea level (150 mmHg) is it?
steps: PIO₂ = FiO₂ × (PB − 47). Subtract water vapour first: 596 − 47 = 549 mmHg.
Multiply by the oxygen fraction: 0.21 × 549 = 115 mmHg.
Compare with sea level: 115 ÷ 150 = 0.77, so PIO₂ is about 23% lower.

steps.title: From thin air to thin blood
steps.text:
Lower PIO₂ means lower oxygen pressure in the lung's air sacs, so the haemoglobin there loads less oxygen: [SaO₂](g:sao2) falls. A pulse oximeter reads it as SpO₂. On arrival your haemoglobin is unchanged, so [arterial O₂ content](g:cao2) (CaO₂ = Hb × 1.34 × SaO₂) falls by the same share as SaO₂.

At rest the loss is modest at moderate altitude, because the top of the O₂–haemoglobin curve is flat. Hard exercise is worse: blood passes the lungs too fast to load fully. In 8 endurance-trained athletes at maximal effort, SpO₂ fell from 89.0% at 300 m to 76.5% at 2,800 m [[c:alt-spo2]].

claims.text: In endurance-trained athletes, SpO₂ at the end of maximal exercise fell from 89.0% at 300 m to 76.5% at 2,800 m.

evidence.quote: Arterial haemoglobin oxygen saturation at test cessation (SpO(2min)) declined from 89.0+/-2.9% at 300 m to 76.5+/-4.0% at 2,800 m (P=0.001).

steps.title: Aerobic power falls in a straight line
steps.text:
In 8 endurance-trained athletes tested in a chamber at six altitudes, [VO₂max](g:vo2max) fell from 66 to 55 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ between 300 and 2,800 m: a straight line, **6.3% per 1,000 m**, with a range of 4.6–7.5% between athletes [[c:alt-vo2-slope]]. Elite cyclists at 2,340 m lost 12.8% on their first day, inside what the line predicts for 2.34 thousand metres (2.34 × 6.3% = 14.7%, or 11–18% across the 4.6–7.5% range) [[c:alt-day1]].

The line was measured between 300 and 2,800 m only. Above that it is a guess, and any single athlete can sit anywhere in the 4.6–7.5% range. Small group, simulated altitude: treat the slope as a good rule of thumb, not a law.

claims.text: In endurance-trained athletes, VO₂max falls linearly, about 6.3% per 1,000 m (range 4.6–7.5%) between 300 and 2,800 m.

evidence.quote: .VO(2max) declined linearly from 66+/-1.6 ml kg(-1) min(-1) at 300 m to 55+/-1.6 ml kg(-1) min(-1) at 2,800 m corresponding to a 6.3% decrease per 1,000 m increasing altitude (range 4.6-7.5%).

claims.text: On their first day at 2,340 m, elite cyclists' VO₂max was 12.8% below sea level.

evidence.quote: On Day 1, VO(2max) and time to exhaustion (at 80% of sea-level maximal power output) decreased by 12.8% (P<0.05) and 25.8% (P<0.05), respectively, compared with the corresponding sea-level values.

steps.title: VO₂max at 2,000 m
steps.problem: An athlete has a sea-level VO₂max of 70 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Using 6.3% per 1,000 m, what do you expect at 2,000 m?
steps: This is the acute value, before any acclimatisation.

steps.title: Performance falls faster, and from low altitude
steps.text:
The same athletes ran to exhaustion at one constant speed (107% of their sea-level VO₂max speed). Their time to exhaustion fell **14.5% per 1,000 m**, more than twice the fall in VO₂max [[c:alt-tte]]. A small loss of aerobic power cuts the time you can hold a fixed, hard speed by a much bigger share. Cyclists at 2,340 m lost 25.8% of time to exhaustion on day 1.

The loss does not wait for high mountains: both VO₂max and performance were already lower at 800 m than at 300 m [[c:alt-low]].

A race is not a fixed-speed test: you slow down instead of dropping out. So the 14.5% is a lab number, not a race-time forecast (see the racing lesson).

claims.text: Time to exhaustion at a constant speed fell about 14.5% per 1,000 m between 300 and 2,800 m in endurance-trained athletes.

evidence.quote: Time to exhaustion (performance) at a constant velocity associated with 107% of sea level .VO(2max) decreased with 14.5% (P<0.001) per 1,000 m altitude between 300 and 2,800 m.

claims.text: In endurance-trained athletes, both VO₂max and performance were already lower at 800 m than at 300 m.

evidence.quote: Both .VO(2max) and performance decreased from 300 to 800 m (P<0.01; P<0.05).

points: Air is 20.9% oxygen at every altitude; pressure falls, so the oxygen pressure falls in proportion. PIO₂ = FiO₂ × (PB − 47 mmHg): about 150 mmHg at sea level, 108 at 2,500 m.
Lower PIO₂ lowers SaO₂ and so CaO₂ by the same share; maximal exercise pulls SpO₂ down further (89% to 76.5% from 300 to 2,800 m).
Endurance-trained athletes lose about 6.3% of VO₂max per 1,000 m (4.6–7.5%), already measurable at 800 m.
Time to exhaustion at a fixed speed falls about 14.5% per 1,000 m: a lab figure, not a race-time forecast.
These numbers come from small studies of 8 athletes; use them as rules of thumb.

variants.stem: At 3,000 m, what share of the air is oxygen?

options.text: About 14%, falling in line with the lower pressure
options.why: Confuses the fraction with the pressure: the pressure falls, the share does not (14% is the tent setting that copies 3,000 m).

options.text: 20.9%, the same as at sea level
options.why: Correct: only the total pressure falls, so the oxygen pressure falls with it.

options.text: About 17%, falling less than the pressure does
options.why: Invents a middle path: the fraction of oxygen is fixed in the whole lower atmosphere.

variants.stem: At 2,500 m, PB is about 560 mmHg. Using FiO₂ = 0.21, what is PIO₂?

options.why: Forgot the 47 mmHg of water vapour: 0.21 × 560.
Forgot to multiply by the oxygen fraction: 560 − 47.
Used the nitrogen share (0.79) instead of oxygen.

variants.stem: At 3,000 m, PB is about 526 mmHg. Using FiO₂ = 0.21, what is PIO₂?

options.why: Forgot the 47 mmHg of water vapour: 0.21 × 526.

options.why: Used the nitrogen share (0.79) instead of oxygen.
Forgot the 47 mmHg of water vapour: 0.21 × 462.
Forgot to multiply by the oxygen fraction: 462 − 47.

variants.stem: Sea-level PIO₂ is 150 mmHg; at 2,500 m it is 108 mmHg (PB 560 against 760). How much lower is the oxygen pressure you breathe?

options.why: Reads the ratio (108 ÷ 150 = 72%) as the fall.
Used the pressure ratio (560 ÷ 760 = 74%): ignores the water vapour that makes the oxygen drop bigger.

variants.solution: 108 ÷ 150 = 0.72, so PIO₂ is 28% lower. The barometric pressure falls only 26% (560 ÷ 760 = 0.74), because the fixed 47 mmHg of water vapour takes a bigger share of thin air.

variants.stem: Sea-level PIO₂ is 150 mmHg; at 3,000 m it is 101 mmHg (PB 526 against 760). How much lower is the oxygen pressure you breathe?

options.why: Reads the ratio (101 ÷ 150 = 67%) as the fall.
Used the pressure ratio (526 ÷ 760 = 69%): ignores the water vapour.

variants.solution: 101 ÷ 150 = 0.67, so PIO₂ is 33% lower. Pressure alone would suggest 31%.

variants.stem: Sea-level PIO₂ is 150 mmHg; at 4,000 m it is 87 mmHg (PB 462 against 760). How much lower is the oxygen pressure you breathe?

options.why: Used the pressure ratio (462 ÷ 760 = 61%): ignores the water vapour.
Reads the ratio (87 ÷ 150 = 58%) as the fall.

variants.solution: 87 ÷ 150 = 0.58, so PIO₂ is 42% lower. Pressure alone would suggest 39%.

variants.stem: Why does SaO₂ fall on arrival at 2,500 m?

options.text: The air sacs hold a lower oxygen pressure, so haemoglobin loads less
options.why: Correct: less pressure pushes less oxygen onto haemoglobin.

options.text: The blood has lost haemoglobin, so there is less to carry oxygen
options.why: Haemoglobin mass is unchanged on arrival: saturation falls, not the amount of haemoglobin.

options.text: The air holds a smaller share of oxygen, so each breath has less
options.why: The share stays 20.9%: the pressure is what changes.

variants.stem: An athlete has Hb 150 g·L⁻¹. At altitude SaO₂ falls from 97% to 80%. What is CaO₂ now (Hb × 1.34 × SaO₂, in mL·L⁻¹)?

options.why: Forgot SaO₂: Hb × 1.34 only.
Used the sea-level saturation (97%) again.
Forgot the 1.34 mL·g⁻¹: Hb × SaO₂.

variants.solution: 150 × 1.34 = 201 mL·L⁻¹ if fully saturated; × 0.80 = 160.8, about 161. At sea level it was 201 × 0.97 = 195, so CaO₂ fell 17.5%.

options.why: Took 6.3% off once, whatever the height gained.

variants.stem: By roughly what share does VO₂max of endurance-trained athletes fall per 1,000 m of acute altitude?

options.why: Far too small: it would make altitude irrelevant to racing.
Correct: 6.3% per 1,000 m in the chamber study (range 4.6–7.5%).
The slope of time to exhaustion at a fixed speed (14.5%), not of VO₂max.
The day-1 fall in time to exhaustion at 2,340 m, not the VO₂max slope.

variants.stem: A cyclist's sea-level time trial takes 60 min. She races at 800 m and wonders if the altitude matters. What does the chamber study suggest?

options.text: Not below about 1,500 m: the air is thick enough
options.why: In the chamber study, VO₂max and performance were already lower at 800 m than at 300 m.

options.text: A small but measurable loss is plausible even at 800 m
options.why: Correct: both measures fell between 300 and 800 m in trained athletes.

options.text: A large loss, as big as at 2,800 m
options.why: The fall is linear: 800 m costs far less than 2,800 m.

variants.stem: The chamber study used 8 endurance-trained athletes in a double-blind design. What limits how far we can use its 6.3% per 1,000 m?

options.text: Double-blind designs are weaker than open ones
options.why: Blinding reduces bias: it is a strength here.

options.text: Only eight athletes in a chamber, and they ranged from 4.6% to 7.5%
options.why: Correct: small sample, chamber exposure and wide individual range limit how precisely it applies to you.

options.text: A straight-line fit proves that every athlete loses the same share
options.why: The reported range (4.6–7.5%) shows athletes differ.
